name: Ashwagandha
lead: Ashwagandha (Withania somnifera), also called Indian ginseng or winter cherry, is an evergreen shrub of the nightshade family whose root powder has been used for centuries in traditional Indian medicine [1]. It is sold as a dietary supplement as root or leaf powder or standardized extracts, marketed as an adaptogen for stress, sleep, vitality, strength and testosterone [1][3].

The main phytochemicals are withanolides, steroidal lactones such as withaferin A, which are structurally similar to ginsenosides, giving rise to the nickname 'Indian ginseng' [1]. In fitness communities it is used for recovery, stress and testosterone support, often alongside other herbal products [14][15].

Meta-analyses of randomised trials report reductions in stress and anxiety scores and a small effect on sleep, but with substantial heterogeneity [3][4][5]. Wikipedia states that current clinical evidence is insufficient to confirm safety or efficacy and notes rare cases of liver injury [1]. A few small trials have examined strength, recovery and endurance outcomes [8][9].
infobox: Avoid in pregnancy; reported rare liver injury [1]

paras: T Nation members list ashwagandha among stacks for stress, sleep and hormone support, including with tongkat ali and fadogia, in training logs, deployment supply lists and TRT recovery logs [14][15][16][17]. A forum post describes a social-media video promoting ashwagandha as a testosterone booster [18].
Ashwagandha root has been used for centuries in Indian traditional medicine [1]. Research has examined stress, anxiety, sleep, thyroid function, cognition and sexual health [3][4][5][11][19][20].

A 2022 meta-analysis of 12 randomised trials (1,002 participants) found that ashwagandha reduced anxiety and stress scores compared with placebo, with very high heterogeneity [3]. A 2024 meta-analysis of nine trials (558 patients) reported significant effects on the Perceived Stress Scale, Hamilton Anxiety Scale and serum cortisol, with mild to moderate adverse events in four trials [4].

A 2021 meta-analysis of five trials (400 participants) found a small but significant effect on sleep, more prominent in people with insomnia, at doses of at least 600 mg/day and for treatment of at least eight weeks [5]. A review of the endocrine system concluded that ashwagandha may have a positive effect on endocrine function but described the literature as heterogeneous [6].

For exercise, a 2015 randomised trial examined muscle strength and recovery with ashwagandha [8], and an 8-week randomised trial in people doing resistance training looked at endurance and VO2max [9]. A systematic review and three-level meta-analysis of ashwagandha and exercise performance has also been published [10]. Trials are small and several use proprietary standardised extracts; readers can consult each trial's funding statement.

Common side effects include diarrhea, headache, sedation and nausea [1]. Ashwagandha has been linked to herb-induced liver injury, particularly in people with preexisting liver conditions, and Wikipedia advises against use during pregnancy or in hormone-sensitive prostate cancer; it may raise testosterone, which could interact with cancer medications [1]. A pharmacological review discusses safety and toxicity aspects [7].

A T Nation user reported trying ashwagandha and not recommending it [21], another said it works best for them when cycled because it seems to lose effectiveness [22], and a third reported a testosterone rise after stopping an antioxidant containing ashwagandha, noting other possible explanations [23].

Withanolides are described as modulating the stress axis, lowering cortisol and affecting GABAergic and inflammatory signalling, according to reviews of its pharmacology [7][6]. Review articles also describe immunomodulatory, anti-inflammatory and neuroprotective effects, largely from preclinical work [7][24].
Ashwagandha has been used for over three thousand years in Indian systems of medicine, as a rasayana (rejuvenator), according to reviews [7][25].

Meta-analyses: stress and anxiety [3][4], sleep [5], exercise performance [10]. Randomised trials: a stress-relief trial of an extract [11], a standardised extract trial on stress hormones [12], subclinical hypothyroidism [13], qualitative analysis of a trial in college students [26], a 2015 trial on strength and recovery [8], and an 8-week resistance training trial on VO2max [9].

Registered trials include footballers' exercise performance (NCT06264986), muscle damage prevention (NCT06900569), adolescent football recovery (NCT07890935), sleep (NCT07151261), sexual health in men and women (NCT05840731, NCT05831241), college student stress (NCT05430685), cognition after chemotherapy (NCT04092647) and a root extract safety study (NCT06261476) [27][28][29][30][19][31][32][20][33].

lore.intro: On T Nation ashwagandha is mentioned mostly in supplement lists and TRT or stress threads, sometimes as a testosterone support and sometimes as a calming herb; experiences are mixed [14][21][22][17].

claims.believers: Social media clips and forum users promote it as a testosterone booster; one user reports taking it with tongkat ali and fadogia [15][18].
claims.experts: A review of ashwagandha and the endocrine system describes possible positive hormonal effects [6]; Wikipedia notes it may increase testosterone [1]. The 2015 trial examined strength and recovery [8].

claims.believers: Users take it for stress and for night-time adrenal issues [22][17].
claims.experts: Meta-analyses report reduced stress, anxiety and cortisol scores, with substantial heterogeneity [3][4].

claims.believers: Posters list it in bedtime stacks with magnesium [37].
claims.experts: A 2021 meta-analysis found a small but significant effect on sleep [5].

claims.believers: Fitness users include it for training support [14][16].
claims.experts: Small trials have examined strength, recovery and endurance outcomes [8][9]; reviews call for larger studies [10].

claims.claim: It loses effectiveness and should be cycled
claims.believers: One TRT-log poster says it works best when cycled because it seems to lose effectiveness [22].
claims.experts: No study cited here examines tolerance or cycling.

claims.claim: Ashwagandha is harmless because it is natural
claims.believers: Users include it routinely in daily stacks [16].
claims.experts: Rare cases of liver injury are documented, and avoidance in pregnancy is advised [1].
